views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Close a limited Phase One text now and treat cancellation of the 15 December List 4B tariffs as a non-negotiable condition of signature, while insisting any rollback of already-imposed duties be simultaneous and proportional. Do not add new tariffs, rare-earth restrictions, or unreliable-entity designations that would give Washington an excuse to walk. Deliver the agricultural, IP, currency, and financial-opening items already outlined in October—but do not enlarge purchase numbers or offer structural industrial-policy concessions until existing 15% and 25% lists start coming off.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material, not existential. List 3 at 25% (10 May) and List 4A at 15% (1 September) already cover the bulk of merchandise exports; Huawei and affiliates remain on the Entity List with U.S. chip/Android supply cut and the temporary general license only extended through 18 November, so the national-champion and 5G self-sufficiency agenda is under direct pressure. Industrial output growth fell to 4.4% in August, a 17-year low, and U.S.-bound exports were reported down more than 12% year-to-date, with factories relocating to Vietnam and Indonesia. African swine fever has driven pork prices up nearly 70% and CPI to 3%, so the growth-plus-food-price squeeze is real. That said, the mid-October U.S. hike was delayed after a Phase One outline (about $40–50bn of U.S. farm goods, IP, currency), China has already issued limited tariff exemptions and farm goodwill, and the 15 December consumer-electronics tranche has not yet landed—so the situation is a high but still-manageable shock, not a legitimacy crisis. Action should therefore stay near zero rather than escalate or concede. Escalation would likely trigger List 4B on phones, laptops and toys (~$156bn) and kill the unsigned text; unilateral extra purchases or a one-sided rollback would spend leverage while Peter Navarro and other U.S. advisers are still publicly denying any agreement to lift existing tariffs. MOFCOM’s 7 November line—phased, same-proportion, simultaneous removal—is the correct bargaining stance. Use Trump’s need for a farm-belt win and the APEC-cancellation delay (possible December signing) to lock Dec-15 cancellation first; keep Meng/Huawei and Xinjiang entity listings outside this commercial tranche so they cannot be used to reopen the whole package.
key_factors: Unsigned Phase One outline (Oct 11) vs still-live 15 Dec List 4B on phones/laptops/toys
Existing 25% List 3 and 15% List 4A already hitting export hubs; factory flight to Vietnam/Indonesia
Huawei Entity List, Android/chip cutoff, TGL only through 18 Nov; not in Phase One
Industrial production 4.4% YoY (Aug) and US-bound exports down >12%; ASF pork shock lifting CPI
US split on tariff rollback (MOFCOM/anonymous US official vs Navarro) — do not pre-concede purchases beyond the October outline
Trump political demand for farm purchases gives China a tradable chip without structural SOE/subsidy surrender

sources_cited.excerpt: After Washington talks, Trump announces a "Phase One" deal in principle: China to buy roughly $40–50B of US agricultural products annually; IP and currency issues also cited. Planned mid-October tariff hike delayed.
List 4A takes effect at 15% (~$110–125B of Chinese imports). China's first tranche of the ~$75B retaliation also takes effect.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
USTR splits List 4: List 4A effective Sept 1; List 4B (including many cell phones, laptops, toys, apparel items) delayed to Dec 15.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
Gao Feng: both sides agreed to remove additional tariffs in phases; if phase one is reached, both should roll back existing additional tariffs in the same proportion simultaneously.
Navarro: there is no agreement at this time to remove any of the existing tariffs as a condition of the phase one deal. Deal still expected to scrap Dec 15 tariffs on ~$156bn if signed.
China pressing to drop Sept 1 15% on ~$125bn and seek relief on 25% lists; Dec 15 fate still under negotiation.
Industrial production increased just 4.4% in August YoY, worse than July's 4.8% and the weakest growth in 17 years.
China's exports to the US dropped by more than 12% this year; manufacturers relocating to Vietnam and Indonesia.
Pork nearly 70% more expensive YoY; CPI to 3% in September from 2.8%.
